name: Levi-Civita Static Cylinder
description: The static vacuum field with cylindrical symmetry, the field outside an infinitely long straight line of mass, which Tullio Levi-Civita found in 1919. It has two parameters, a mass per unit length and an angular deficit about the axis, and it is flat with no mass and again where the mass parameter is one half.
convention: The mass parameter $\sigma$ is dimensionless, $G/c^2$ times the mass per unit length of the source where it is small. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The ninth of Tullio Levi-Civita's notes on Einsteinian $ds^2$ in Newtonian fields, a series he began in 1917, appeared in 1919 and treats the static vacuum field with cylindrical symmetry [levicivita1919, levicivita2011b, maccallum2011]. Levi-Civita introduced the analog of the logarithmic potential of Newtonian gravity and found the other metric coefficients from the vacuum Einstein equations [levicivita2011b, maccallum2011]. For small $\sigma$ the field is that of an infinitely long homogeneous line of mass in Newton's theory, with $\sigma$ its mass per unit length, as Levi-Civita noticed himself [herrera2001]. Werner Israel confirmed in 1977 that $\sigma$ is the mass per unit length [israel1977, maccallum2011]. Levi-Civita's metric is a member of the class of static axisymmetric vacuum solutions Hermann Weyl gave in 1917, and it is the static class of the family Edward Kasner published in 1921 [weyl1917, kasner1921, maccallum2011].¶The solution holds two independent parameters, $\sigma$ and $C$, as L. Marder established in 1958 [marder1958, herrera2001]. A change of coordinates takes $C$ to $1$ locally, and with $\phi$ running once round the axis $C$ fixes the angular deficit there [maccallum2011]. William Bonnor pointed out in 1979 that the constant has a global topological meaning and cannot be removed by scale transformations [bonnor1979, herrera2001]. At $\sigma = 0$ the spacetime is flat, and with $\phi$ periodic it is the spacetime of a cosmic string [maccallum2011, vilenkin1981]. The metric is also the limit of the $\gamma$ metric, whose potential is that of a finite rod, as the length of the rod tends to infinity [herrera1999, maccallum2011].¶The curvature is infinite on the axis $\rho = 0$ for every $\sigma$ except $0$ and $1/2$, where the spacetime is flat [dasilva1995]. At $\sigma = 1/2$ it is flat spacetime in the coordinates of a uniformly accelerated frame [wang1997]. M. F. A. da Silva, Luis Herrera, Filipe Paiva, and Nilton Santos found in 1995 that the metric is of Petrov type I except at $\sigma = -1/2$, $1/4$, and $1$, where it is of type D and has one more symmetry [dasilva1995]. At $\sigma = -1/2$ that symmetry is a rotation in the plane of $z$ and $\phi$, and the metric is locally the plane symmetric vacuum Abraham Taub found in 1951 [wang1997, taub1951]. At $\sigma = 1/4$ it is a Lorentz boost that mixes $t$ and $\phi$ [wang1997]. Far from its axis Melvin's magnetic universe approaches the Levi-Civita metric with $\sigma = 1$ [kastor2021].¶A particle on a circular geodesic moves past the static observers at one speed $W$ whatever its radius, with $W^2 = 2\sigma/(1 - 2\sigma)$ in units of the speed of light, as round a line of mass in Newton's theory [dasilva1995, herrera2001]. That speed reaches the speed of light at $\sigma = 1/4$, and Ronald Gautreau and R. B. Hoffman demonstrated in 1969 that no circular geodesic is timelike for $\sigma \geq 1/4$ [gautreau1969, dasilva1995]. Bonnor and M. A. P. Martins conjectured in 1991 that the metric does not represent an infinite line of mass if $\sigma \geq 1/4$ [bonnormartins1991, dasilva1995]. In 1992 Bonnor and W. Davidson matched it to a cylinder of perfect fluid with $\sigma$ above $1/4$ and below $1/2$ [bonnordavidson1992, dasilva1995]. A cylinder of dust with equal numbers of particles circling the axis in each sense is a source for $0 \leq \sigma \leq 1/2$, as da Silva, Herrera, Paiva, and Santos found in 1995 [dasilva1995]. For $-1/2 < \sigma < 1/2$ the source can be a cylinder of perfect fluid and for $|\sigma| > 1/2$ a wall, with the sign of the fluid's density that of $\sigma$, as Thomas Philbin found in 1996 [philbin1996].¶A cylindrical shell of anisotropic fluid that satisfies the energy conditions is a source for $0 \leq \sigma \leq 1$, as Anzhong Wang, da Silva, and Santos found in 1997 [wang1997]. Herrera, Santos, Antonio Teixeira, and Wang showed in 2001 that at $\sigma = 1/2$ the axial and angular coordinates switch meaning, and gave a shell that satisfies the energy conditions for every $\sigma \geq 0$ [herrera2001]. By Israel's definition the energy per unit length of their shell is $\sigma/(4\sigma^2 - 2\sigma + 1)$, which is greatest at $\sigma = 1/2$, where it is $1/2$, and falls to zero as $\sigma \to \infty$ [herrera2001, israel1977]. The Levi-Civita spacetime has no event horizon [herrera2001]. In 1999 Bonnor wrote that "the Levi-Civita spacetime continues to puzzle relativists" [bonnor1999, bicak2004]. Jiří Bičák, Tomáš Ledvinka, Bernd Schmidt, and Martin Žofka demonstrated in 2004 that static cylinders of perfect fluid with their Levi-Civita exteriors exist as unique global solutions for a fairly general equation of state, and that only special cylinders have an exterior with $C = 1$ [bicak2004].

coordinates.name: Weyl

parameters.description: Mass parameter, dimensionless; for small $\sigma$ the mass per unit length of the source is $\sigma c^2/G$, and the spacetime is flat at $\sigma = 0$ and at $\sigma = 1/2$
Conicity parameter, dimensionless; with $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$ it fixes the angular deficit about the axis, and no change of coordinates removes it

coordinates.convention: We use Weyl's coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, and we evaluate $\rho^{4\sigma}$ and $\rho^{4\sigma(2\sigma - 1)}$ with $\rho$ in a fixed unit of length, so they are dimensionless. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Kasner

parameters.description: Exponent along $\phi$, $p_\phi = (1 - 2\sigma)/\Sigma$; the two constraints leave one free exponent
Radius of the circle about the axis at unit $r$, a length, $\ell = \Sigma^{p_\phi}/C$ in the unit of length chosen

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \phi, z)$ with $r$ the proper distance from the axis, $r = \rho^{\Sigma}/\Sigma$ with $\Sigma = 4\sigma^2 - 2\sigma + 1$, and $t$ and $z$ those of Weyl's coordinates multiplied by constants, and we evaluate the powers $r^{2p_i}$ with $r$ in a fixed unit of length, so they are dimensionless. The exponents obey $p_t + p_z + p_\phi = 1$ and $p_t^2 + p_z^2 + p_\phi^2 = 1$, and every component assumes both conditions. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
